{{Short description|Theorem in graph theory}}
In [[mathematics]], '''Veblen's theorem''', introduced by {{harvs|txt|last=Veblen|first=Oswald|year=1912|authorlink=Oswald Veblen}},  states that the set of edges of a finite [[graph (discrete mathematics)|graph]] can be written as a union of  disjoint [[cycle (graph theory)|simple cycles]] if and only if every vertex has even [[degree (graph theory)|degree]]. Thus, it is closely related to the theorem of {{harvtxt|Euler|1736}} that a finite graph has an [[Euler tour]] (a single non-simple cycle that covers the edges of the graph) if and only if it is [[connectivity (graph theory)|connected]] and every vertex has even degree. Indeed, a representation of a graph as a union of simple cycles may be obtained from an Euler tour by repeatedly splitting the tour into smaller cycles whenever there is a repeated vertex. However, Veblen's theorem applies also to disconnected graphs, and can be generalized to [[infinite graph]]s in which every vertex has finite degree.{{sfn|Sabidussi|1964}}

If a [[countably infinite]] graph ''G'' has no odd-degree vertices, then it may be written as a union of disjoint (finite) simple cycles if and only if every finite subgraph of ''G'' can be extended (by including more edges and vertices from ''G'') to a finite Eulerian graph. In particular, every countably infinite graph with only one [[end (graph theory)|end]] and with no odd vertices can be written as a union of disjoint cycles.{{sfn|Sabidussi|1964}}
